paragraphs.heading: A perfect umpire
paragraphs.edited: Baseball, the American pastime. Stolen bases, home runs, grand slams, hot dogs and nachos. These are some of the things that make a baseball game fun. Part of the experience, of course, is yelling at the umpires. And let's face it, they're going to make a lot of mistakes. They're human. When they make a bad call or they miss a call, we let them have it. But what if there were a perfect umpire? This umpire got calls correct one hundred percent of the time.

When they make a bad call or they miss a call, we let them have it. But what if there were a perfect umpire? This umpire got calls correct one hundred percent of the time.

paragraphs.heading: Would we listen to him?
paragraphs.edited: You know, with modern technology today we can almost do this. We can tell if a pitch is a strike or a ball, or if a runner is safe or out. If an umpire had that knowledge, would we listen to this umpire? The answer is, of course we would. Now, a call from our perspective might seem like they got it wrong, but given that this umpire is correct 100 percent of the time, we would always know that the umpire got the call right. Human beings differ wildly on all sorts of social, ethical, scientific, and theological issues. But what if there was an umpire that was always correct, especially on spiritual issues? This umpire never got it wrong. Would we listen to that person?

paragraphs.heading: A question to a room of skeptics
paragraphs.edited: Some time ago, I went with my wife and my pastor to meet a group of skeptics, atheists, and agnostics. Toward the end of the meeting, my pastor asked a really interesting question. He said to this group of people who don't believe in God, if there were a God, would his opinion be more valuable than yours? And to me, the answer seems obvious. If there's a God who spoke all of creation into existence and knows everything, then of course his opinion is more valuable than mine. This group of people hesitated, and eventually they said no. Even if there were a God, his opinion would not be more important or authoritative than theirs.

paragraphs.heading: Who do we trust?
paragraphs.edited: This gets to the heart of the matter of authority in our world. Who do we trust? Now, we would trust a perfect umpire, and this umpire would have authority because he or she would never make the wrong call. Well, the same is true with God. If there is a God, and this God by definition is self-existent, eternal, perfectly good, loving, and knows everything, then by definition this God is going to make the right call. Now, it might seem from our perspective that God has made the wrong call, but if we stopped and focused on the character of God, we would know that the problem is not with the call, that the problem is with our perspective.

paragraphs.heading: A conversation with a former pastor
paragraphs.edited: Recently I was invited to participate in a public conversation with a former pastor who's become an atheist, and he asked some good questions, such as, how could a loving God send somebody to hell? Or why would God have his chosen people in the Old Testament engage in warfare? These are thoughtful questions that every Christian needs to wrestle with. But rather than answer his particular questions, as important as they are, I wanted to frame the conversation differently.

paragraphs.edited: I said that any adequate worldview has to account for certain big features in reality. Any adequate worldview has to explain certain big questions we have about life, such as, why is the universe so exquisitely fine-tuned for life? What best explains the origin of information in DNA? And what worldview can account for the origin of things like objective beauty, morality, and free will? The reality is that atheism can't answer any of the big questions of life. But Christianity can.

paragraphs.heading: God's word as the authority
paragraphs.edited: What this means is that if Christianity is true, then we can trust that God is the authority for all of life. Are there some tough questions that remain, like this pastor asked? Yes. But we can trust that God exists and God is good, and that he has reasons, even if he doesn't always fully reveal those reasons to us. Jesus believed that God's word was authoritative for all of life. That's why, when he was asked tough questions, he often responded by saying, have you not heard, or have you not read? He was appealing to the Old Testament, because he believed that God's word was reliable and authoritative in everything that it taught.

Who are we going to look to as the authority?

paragraphs.heading: Will you trust him?
paragraphs.edited: The only way we can be right with God and experience the abundant life that Jesus promised is by following God's guide for our lives as found in the Scriptures. Many people in our world will say that the Bible is antiquated or that God is a cosmic killjoy, but this isn't true. God's commandments and teachings exist for our good. God has our best in mind. So regardless of how you feel or how things appear to be in your life, the question is, will you trust God as the ultimate authority in your life? It's hard to imagine a question more important than this.
